title: One Hundred Percent Restitution: $1.212 Billion Back, and an Admission of Liability
participants: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was taken was customer money held under a statutory protection. The CFTC’s complaint charged MF Global and other defendants "with unlawful use of customer funds", and charged the firm, "a registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM), with violating provisions of the Commodity Exchange Act and CFTC Regulations intended to protect FCM customer funds and requiring diligent supervision by registrants."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was of segregation itself — the rule that a futures commission merchant holds customer property apart from its own. The charge is not of a bad trade but of using funds that were not the firm’s to use, and of failing in the supervision the registration carries with it.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The shortfall became visible only at failure, which is what segregation rules exist to prevent: the restitution ordered was "to ensure customers recover their losses sustained when MF Global failed in 2011", and the trustee had to seek permission "to pay restitution in full to customers to remedy any shortfall with funds of the MF Global general estate."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: There was no windfall; there was a hole, and it was filled. The consent order required "$1.212 billion in restitution to customers", and the acting enforcement director framed the objective as "100 percent restitution ... to satisfy customer losses".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The disposition is unusually un-whitewashed for this atlas and the dossier should say so. The order was entered by a federal judge, it imposed a $100 million civil penalty subordinated to customer and priority-creditor recovery, and — unlike most settlements in this file — "In the consent Order, MF Global admits to the allegations pertaining to its liability based on the acts and omissions of its employees". As at the date of the release, "The CFTC's litigation continues against the remaining defendants: MF Global Holdings Ltd., Jon S. Corzine, and Edith O'Brien" — pending matters whose outcomes are not sourced here and are not asserted.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The futures commission merchant regime: customer funds segregated by rule, with the firm permitted to invest them within limits and the protection resting on the firm’s own compliance.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-MF Global tightening of customer-funds protection and residual-interest rules, and a consent order in which an FCM admitted liability rather than neither admitting nor denying.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Customer property was the cheapest liquidity available to a firm under funding stress; using it relieved the stress that made it attractive; and the protection that should have prevented it depended on the same firm reporting its own compliance.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That MF Global’s customers were simply robbed and never made whole, and that nobody admitted anything or paid a penny.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Both halves are contradicted by the order. Customers were made whole: the consent order required $1.212 billion in restitution and the trustee obtained permission to pay customers in full from the general estate, with the enforcement division describing the aim as 100 percent restitution. And an admission was made: "In the consent Order, MF Global admits to the allegations pertaining to its liability based on the acts and omissions of its employees" — which is rarer than the usual neither-admit-nor-deny formula and should be reported as such. What the document does not establish is anything about the individuals: the litigation against MF Global Holdings, Jon S. Corzine and Edith O'Brien was continuing as at this release, and nothing about its outcome is sourced here.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A CFTC complaint of 27 June 2013 charging MF Global with unlawful use of customer funds and with violating Commodity Exchange Act provisions and CFTC regulations protecting FCM customer funds and requiring diligent supervision. A federal court consent order entered on 8 November 2013 by Judge Victor Marrero in the Southern District of New York requiring $1.212 billion in restitution to customers, and imposing a $100 million civil monetary penalty payable only after customers and priority creditors are paid. The firm’s admission of liability for the acts and omissions of its employees. The trustee’s bankruptcy-court permission to pay customers in full from the general estate. And continuing litigation, as at 18 November 2013, against MF Global Holdings Ltd., Jon S. Corzine and Edith O'Brien.

citations.title: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, "Federal Court in New York Orders MF Global Inc. to Pay over $1 Billion in Restitution to Customers", Release 6776-13, 18 November 2013
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from cftc.gov. The CFTC "obtained a federal court consent Order against Defendant MF Global Inc. (MF Global) requiring it to pay $1.212 billion in restitution to customers of MF Global to ensure customers recover their losses sustained when MF Global failed in 2011." The order was "entered on November 8, 2013 by U.S. District Court Judge Victor Marrero of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York", and "also imposes a $100 million civil monetary penalty on MF Global, to be paid after MF Global has fully paid customers and certain other creditors entitled to priority under bankruptcy law." On the shortfall being made good: "The Trustee for MF Global obtained permission from the bankruptcy court to pay restitution in full to customers to remedy any shortfall with funds of the MF Global general estate." THE ADMISSION, which distinguishes this from a neither-admit-nor-deny settlement: "In the consent Order, MF Global admits to the allegations pertaining to its liability based on the acts and omissions of its employees as set forth in the consent Order and the Complaint." The underlying complaint, filed 27 June 2013, charged MF Global and other defendants "with unlawful use of customer funds", and charged the firm, "a registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM), with violating provisions of the Commodity Exchange Act and CFTC Regulations intended to protect FCM customer funds and requiring diligent supervision by registrants." The release records that "The CFTC's litigation continues against the remaining defendants: MF Global Holdings Ltd., Jon S. Corzine, and Edith O'Brien" — as at the date of this release those were pending matters, and nothing about their outcome is sourced here. Acting Enforcement Director Gretchen Lowe is quoted: "Division staff have worked tirelessly to ensure that 100 percent restitution be awarded to satisfy customer losses."
